planting.note: Set bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally against a warm south-facing wall. Isabel is grown for its dark rose-pink, wavy-petaled umbels held on bare stems well ahead of the strap-shaped foliage.

directions: Set bulbs shallowly in gritty, lean soil in full sun, since Isabel flowers most reliably when roots are congested and slightly baked over summer. Bare flower stalks emerge in early autumn topped with dark rose-pink, recurved blossoms, with the strappy leaves following once the blooms fade and persisting through winter before summer dormancy. Leave clumps undisturbed for several years to build up flowering strength, and withhold water almost entirely once foliage dies back in late spring. In climates colder than zone 7, grow in containers that can be moved under cover for winter or mulch heavily where planted in the open ground.

common_name: Leia Pineapple Lily (Compact Early-Blooming Raspberry-Pink Aloha Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after the soil has warmed in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Leia is a compact Aloha Lily series hybrid bred from Eucomis vandermerwei that flowers several weeks earlier in the season than most other pineapple lily cultivars.

directions: Plant bulbs about three inches deep once danger of frost has passed, in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Leia forms a tidy, compact clump of glossy, wavy-margined green leaves and sends up sturdy spikes topped with burgundy-maroon buds that open to raspberry-pink flowers carrying a faint coconut-like scent, blooming earlier in summer than most pineapple lily selections. Its dwarf habit makes it well suited to containers and the front of a mixed border, and the flower spikes persist attractively for weeks before the seed heads take over the ornamental display. Divide congested clumps in spring only when flowering declines, since eucomis generally bloom best when left undisturbed for several years.

common_name: Forked Watsonia (Tall Orange-Red Cape Bugle Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; like most summer-growing watsonias, this Cape species roots in over the cool season and sends up its tall flower spikes the following late spring to early summer.

directions: Named for the South African forester and surveyor Henri Fourcade, this species produces some of the tallest flower spikes in the genus, reaching four to six feet on rocky sandstone slopes of the Eastern and Western Cape. Elongated, branching spikes carry tubular orange-to-red blooms in tidy rows above a fan of broad, sword-shaped leaves, opening in sequence up the stem over several weeks and making excellent, long-lasting cut flowers. Give it full sun and soil that drains well in winter but does not dry out completely during the growing season, and protect corms from hard freezes since it is markedly less cold-hardy than Watsonia borbonica. Established clumps can be left in place for years in mild, frost-free gardens, multiplying steadily by cormlets without needing regular division.
